speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: RATIONING OF BEER AND SPIRITS-ONTARIO AND QUEBEC-STATEMENT OF PREMIER DREW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement with reference to an announcement recently made by the premier of Ontario concerning the ration of spirits in
Alcoholic Beverages-Rationing

that province. Colonel Drew referred to the difference in the amounts authorized by the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and stated:
There may be some good explanation for this striking contrast in ration, but there can be no doubt of the effect of this situation upon the minds of those who come in contact with it.
Under P.C. 11374, the wartime alcoholic beverages order, the provinces are restricted to receiving each year for sale seventy per cent of the spirits which they received during the year ended October 31, 1942.
Each province receives the same percentage. All are treated alike, and there is therefore no foundation for any suggestion of discrimination.
Although this fact is well known, efforts are constantly being made to create an impression that Quebec is receiving preferential treatment over other provinces, particularly Ontario. It will be noted that although Quebec received 13,828 proof gallons of spirits more than Ontario, Ontario consumed over nine million gallons of beer more than Quebec. Expressing it in another way, Quebec received 1-2 per cent more spirits, while Ontario received 32-4 per cent more beer.
One obvious reason for the discrepancy in the ration between, provinces lies in the variation in the number of permits issued. I observe from a recent advertisement of the liquor control board of Ontario that in January, 1943, when the permits issued by the province totalled 155,295 the monthly ration was 160 ounces. According to the same source, in March, 1944, the province had issued 1,282,938 permits, and the ration at that time was 26 ounces. I do not know how many permits are outstanding in Ontario at the present time. In one Ontario city a man has recently been prosecuted for having no less than 63 permits. The best answer to Premier Drew's allusions to the relative ration of Ontario and Quebec seems to be

made by the chairman of the Ontario liquor commission, who says in the advertisement, "It is a problem in simple arithmetic," and goes on to state that:
The increase in the number of permits and the extent to which permit holders are purchasing spirits each month makes it necessary to reduce the amount which can be purchased by permit holders in Ontario.
Attempts are also being made to becloud the issue by drawing attention to the stocks of spirits which are held in warehouses. As far as the federal government is concerned, there has never been any suggestion that the restriction placed on the consumption of spirits was attributable to a shortage of supply. Minister of Munitions and Supply always has one answer for everything, and that is ''politics". I was about to say that I encounter people from time to time who think that if some matter is raised with respect to the farmers, major importance should not be attached to it. Now I happen to know, ns does the hon. member for Peterborough West, that the question the hon. member asked relates to a matter of great urgency, particularly in western Ontario and in the district from which he comes. speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO RELEASE OF AMMUNITION FOR DESTRUCTION OF VERMIN

The distribution of ammunition

for farmers is a matter for the wartime prices and trade board. The ammunition industry of this country is operating at full capacity and has been doing so for a very long time, but the ammunition is being used for other purposes than the shooting of small animals in Canada. I am sure that if any ammunition can be released without jeopardizing the war effort it will be released. This is not a matter of immediate urgency; it has been before departments of government for the last eight months at least, and we are doing the best we can to meet the situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, June 2, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain, sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state'of war-Mr. Usley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Old age pensions and pensions to the blind, $6,942,250.

A few days ago the Minister of Finance made a statement in respect of old age pensions having to be paid back from the estates of the old age pensioners, and pointed out that the policy was left pretty much with provincial departments of finance. It is my understanding that in the past that has been the regulation. Just what advantage the provinces have taken of it, I do not know, but I do know the effect on old age pensioners.
When applying for a pension the applicant is asked to sign a document which hands over as collateral for his pension the little house or home in which he has had considerable pride. Is this a charge against the entire estate, or is it a charge against the property value of the estate up to the amount the minister mentioned? I ask this question because during the last victory loan campaign I was asked if war savings bonds would be considered part of the estate and subject to collection by the provinces in the event of the death of a pensioner. I could not answer the question, nor did I have time on that occasion to get in touch with the minister. Perhaps he will reply to the numerous speeches which have been made, and when he does I would ask him to include an answer to the question I have now asked.
I have always maintained that old age pensions should be paid to our aged mothers and fathers by right of their Canadian heritage. It is my belief that if the nation is to reach the status of a glorious Canadian people, one thing we have to do is to recognize as a right of Canadian citizenship the giving of adequate old age pensions to those who have pioneered in the country, to those who have spent their lives to make the kind of Canada we want.
I should like now to make some observations in respect of the speech delivered on Friday evening by the Minister of Labour. I have a good deal of .respect for him, and therefore I am not going to criticize him personally. He is much bigger than I am, and I must be careful of what I say about him. However, as this is a land of free speech I suppose I have some rights when I criticize words spoken by him. This is what he said:
I think I would advocate contributory old age pensions. I believe that pensions should be paid-I speak now as an individual-to the people of this country by right.
A statement of that kind is, to my mind, a misnomer. One does not have to talk about paying to people by right something that is owed to them. That goes without saying. I do not talk about this country paying me my indemnity by right. By law I am paid so much to indemnify me for what I may lose in my constituency by becoming a member of parliament. I do not have to say that that is paid to me by right; it goes without saying. That is one criticism I would .make of the minister's speech.
Conversely to that, what the minister has in mind, of course, is that anything given to our old age pensioners, anything they receive by way of a gift, anything which does not come out of a fund to which they have contributed, is not their right.
War Appropriation-Finance

If I may correct my hon. friend, I do not think he wishes to misinterpret what I said. I still think it is theirs by right, but I think if one helps to pay for a thing, at least he has something to say about how it should be disposed of. That is not theory.

I do not think the minister has contradicted what I said. If we want to have a Canada such as we should have, then in my view anyone who puts his life into the building of Canada, anyone who has lived as a citizen of our country, should have by right of citizenship and by right of his Canadian heritage an adequate pension paid to him, without his paying for it for years before he reaches old age. If there is a contributory form of old age pensions then we are only paying back to the old age pensioner what he has contributed to the fund in his younger days.
I wish to draw this to the attention of the Minister of Labour, and I want to be as logical as I can. I think he is a logical man and I think he will follow this argument. The Minister of Labour is charged with the problem of finding employment. Very well. Any individual who contributes to old age pension, unemployment insurance, life insurance, or any other form of social services or means by which he can be helped later on, does so out of his wages or salary; therefore he has less to spend on that which is produced. If he has less to spend on that which is produced, then the production to that extent is not sold; and if you follow it to its logical conclusion it means that eventually men are laid off. If they are laid off, their purchasing power is still further reduced and there is more unemployment. I want the minister to think of that, because if it is followed to its logical conclusion there will be less employment in this country. Taking a long range view of this old age pension problem, we see that it will stretch forward into the years of our post-war life, the years when the production of civilian goods will be speeded up, and it will not be very long before we are in the same position as that in which we found ourselves a few years ago when there was what was commonly known as a period of overproduction.
A man and his wife, walking down a street, look into a shop window. Perhaps it is a furniture store. The wife notices a nice piece of furniture, a chesterfield or something of the kind. She would like that beautiful piece of furniture to grace her home. She says, "Well, Pa, what about it? Do you think we shall be able to buy it?" Pa figures it out and he says, "Well, now I don't know, Ma,

if I can. I don't think we can buy it now. I have my unemployment insurance, which of course, is a tax. I have some taxes to pay on the property; and then I do not get much of a wage. There is the income tax, and that reminds me that I did not pay my radio licence fee, which is another tax. I shall be having that man after me if I do not pay it. Then of course there is the old age pension tax; this contributory scheme. Oh, no, Ma, I'm afraid I won't be able to buy that piece of furniture for you. I shall have to wait until we get old; then I may be able to squeeze out a little bit." That is the position. By the time this, that and the other thing are taken from a man's wages, how is he to buy back the production of industry? Industry becomes slowed up, and the first thing you know we have a period of unemployment on our hands.
Let me read what the minister said on Friday night as reported on page 3503 of Hansard:
We hear people talk about non-contributory unemployment insurance and non-contributory this and non-contributory something else. Whether you like it or not, anything and everything that is paid by the state is a okarge on the living standards of the people of this dominion or any other nation.
I say to the minister that I for one do not believe that statement. I suggest that he is thinking too far back. He is not thinking in terms of a modern technological age when we are able to produce more than we can consume. All I have to do is to bring to his attention the pre-war years, or, if you like, the post-war years when there will be over-production. People have been paid their wages, and for the purpose of my illustration there may even be a period when everybody is more or less employed. But through the advancement of technological skill we are able to produce an abundance. Goods pile up. If there is a surplus of production, does the minister say that if we organize our economic system through a financial accountancy to distribute that surplus to our aged mothers and fathers it will depreciate the standard of living in this country? I should like to have him answer that some time if he cares to.
He would rather not.

It is true that in years gone by there was destruction of our surplus when people were in need. If ever I thought this world was a lunatic asylum it was at that time. I recall reading of a shipload of oranges going out from Liverpool and being dumped into the sea when little children in England needed them. Instead of feeding them to the

War Appropriation-Finance
children they fed them to the fish. Of course, economists from such schools as the London School of Economics, if you like, would say: But the children did not have any money to pay for them. Well, that is true; neither did the fish, but the fish got them and the children who needed them had to go without. We all remember the coffee from Brazil that was burned and dumped into the sea. We all recall blankets being destroyed and cotton ploughed under in the United States. Does the minister say that if instead of destroying those goods we arranged our economy in such a way as to distribute them to the aged and the needy it would reduce the standard of living in this country? That is something for him to think about.
The minister in his remarks on Friday night (vent on to say:
Whether you like it or not,-*
That is a nice preface to a statement.
[DOT]-anything and everything

There is a positiveness about this. He is so sure about it.
-everything that is paid iby the state is a charge on the living standards of the people of this dominion or any other nation.
Then listen to this:	.
History has proven that pride is the backbone of a nation.
Well, for a little while I am going to talk about pride. I am going to ask the minister if it is anything to be proud of when our economic arrangement is such that we have to destroy goods instead of distributing them.

I am sure my hon.
friend is not suggesting that I said we should destroy goods.
No; the minister said that people could not get something for nothing. We cannot give them the goods, so if they cannot be sold they must be destroyed; that is the logic of it.
That is the weakness of your argument.

No, it is not my argument, and I do not know whether it is the minister's, but that is actually what has been done and it is exactly what will have to be done if the present economic arrangement is not changed. There is only one other way to deal with it; that is to give people enough purchasing power over and above wages to buy the surplus of goods, and you can start with the old age pensioner. As the hon. member for Jasper-Edson suggests, we are giving fifty per cent of our production to the enemy now and making no bones about
it. I heard a story once about little Johnny. When he was a small boy he wanted a tricycle, but his father could not buy him one because he had no money. When Johnny got a little bigger he wanted a bicycle, but his father could not buy it for him because he had no money. A little later he thought he would like a car, since he was growing up, but his father could not buy one, and if Johnny wanted a car he would have to make it out of some old junk. Finally the time came when he did not want to live on his father any longer, so he began to tramp the roads of the country, to ride the rods, frying eggs by the side of the railroad track in the midst of abundance. Then war broke out; economic necessity laid hold of him and said, "Johnny, how would you like to have three meals a day and a suit or two suits of clothes?" Johnny replied, "What do you mean?" "Well, come with me and sign on the dotted line and you will get them." So he went and signed on the dotted line and got three meals a day and two suits of clothes. Then one day they came along and said, "Johnny, how would you like a nice education?" Johnny replied, "Are you going to give me a good education?" "Yesv we will give you an education that will cost $25,000." But Johnny said, "I could not possibly afford that." The reply was, "Oh, you don't need to pay for it; we will pay for it." So they took him and made him a pilot, at a cost of $25,000. After that they said, "How would you like a nice railroad trip?" He replied, "Well, I had many of those railroad trips before the war, and I got very tired of them; I used to ride the rods." "Well, you will not have to ride the rods now; we will even give you a berth to sleep in." "You are going to give it to me?" "Yes, we will give it to you." So he went all the way to Halifax. Then they asked, "Would you like a nice trip over the ocean?" and they took him over the ocean to a bomber field in England and said, "Look at that machine." He said, "Boy, isn't she a big one?" Then they said, "Here is a big bomber; how would you like to fly it?" "I couldn't afford to fly that; I could not buy the gasoline to fly even a mile." "Oh, that makes no difference; jump in." So Johnny jumped in and began to fly it all round. Eventually they said, "How would you like to fly over Germany?" "Well, I wouldn't mind; it has not cost me anything so far." But before leaving for German}' that afternoon they wheeled out the bombs and Johnny asked, "What are those?" "Oh, these are bombs." "How much did they cost?" "Oh, we couldn't tell you; thousands of dollars. Now we want you to take them over to Germany, and when you

War Appropriation-Finance
get over there we want you to give them to the Germans." "What, give them to the Germans? Are you not going to charge anything for them?" So he took them over Germany and gave the bombs to the Germans. As he was flying back be thought, "My, that is a great idea. I never knew they could give things away like that. Why could we not have a' system after the war under which we could fly over Canada and, instead of dropping bombs, drop washing machines, furniture and things like that?"
That is the logical sequence. In time of war we are able to give a large part of our production to the enemy, but we are not able to give any of our surplus to our aged people in time of peace. When the minister talks of pride I tell him that I will have plenty of pride in a nation that provides for its aged people out of the abundance of its production and its surpluses. Suppose we came to a place in our economy when we provided all these things for our people; when, as they grew older, they retired on an adequate pension, not a pinch-penny $25 or even $30 a month, but $50 or more if necessary. Raise the ante, as long as there is a surplus of production. Imagine the minister and his friends who hold the same philosophy saying, " Well, I do not know whether or not I am proud of that. I think perhaps I had better go to some other country where they charge us in our youth for that which we may get if we live long enough to receive it." He ridicules the idea of something for nothing. I wonder if the minister has ever considered that some of the most precious things of life are given us for nothing. The very air we breathe we get for nothing, unless we want to listen over it; then we have to pay.
It is not a good thing to mention that to the minister.
I want him to see if there is anything wrong in the philosophy of something for nothing. The energy that comes from the sun; the rain-these are given to all, rich and poor alike.
It has to be harnessed.

That is true; I am only saying that these things are given to us for nothing, and they are given to rich and poor alike. Let us take another example, if the hon. member for York-Sunbury objects to that one. Here is a youqg man who inherits a million dollars. If he holds the views of the minister he will say, " Oh, pride forbid; I could not take that, for it is something I am getting for nothing." All I say is that I have not a rich uncle or a rich father and mother,

but I belong to a rich country. I belong to a country whose citizens have a heritage far greater than that of any other country in the world.
At page 3503 the minister goes on to say:
I have given what I 'have always considered to he my philosophy of life. It is as old as history itself.
Of course; that is what is wrong with it.
And remember this, that any state which started out to kid the people that it was giving something away for nothing has ended up in the ash can.
The hon. gentleman starts off as Minister of Labour; then he takes the part of a great economist, and now he has become a great historian.
It may be that we now have a new formula; I do not know. I sincerely hope, with all my being, that we have. But human nature being what it is, and in the light of history, there is reason for doubt. One could read the history-*
Then he refers to Carthage, Rome, Greece and "other civilizations and nations". Surely the Minister of Labour is not going to compare modern civilization with bygone dynasties. Some of us have read a little history. Those days were days of scarcity; and furthermore, there was a vast distinction between the rich, or the aristocracy, and the slaves who laboured by the sweat of their brow to provide for the rich. That day may not be completely gone economically, but I am certain that the minister cannot compare our modern age, our modern country and our modern civilization with bygone days and bygone nations. I think that is enough for the Minister of Labour.
A little later I was interested in listening to the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I usually enjoy his speeches because he is quite human and understanding, but I must confess I was a little amused when he tangled with the Minister of Finance over the matter of taxation or contributions given to this or that fund in New Zealand and here. I could not help thinking to myself, "Are they fighting over which system of taxation is the best?" I was tempted to say, "Why any taxation at all?" I say that with all sincerity. I do not believe there is any need for the extreme taxation that we have had in this country. I am not going to criticize what is happening at the moment, because we know that there is a vast depreciation in time of war in all civilian goods and that much of our money must be spent for munitions of war and goods of that nature. I am talking of normal times, when we get back to our quiet, peaceful life. In those days I see no reason for the taxation that has bled the people of this country white.

War Appropriation-Finance
In this connection I want to read from a book written by Major Douglas, "Monopoly of Credit". I make no apology for quoting any first-rank siocial crediter.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is proposing to discuss a matter dealt with by Major Douglas. We are dealing with old age pensions in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have no doubt that a large part of the matter dealt with by the hon. member for Macleod has been out of order. We have been discussing old age pensions, and I hope that hon. members will keep within the orbit of the item.
I am sure I will keep within the rules. Most of my time has been taken up in criticizing the Minister of Labour.
Stay with the Minister of Labour.

If I was out of order, then he must have been out of order. I intend to refer to contributory old age pension schemes, which are a form of taxation. I shall soon be finished, so that the hon. member who has raised the objection need not worry. Major Douglas says-
Who is Major Douglas?
My hon. friend knows.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not believe the committee is discussing a contributory old age pension scheme; it is discussing the operation of old age pensions in Canada. I do not see how the discussion of that type of scheme would be relevant.

I am not going to argue the point, but I will say that on Friday night the Minister of Labour went out of his way to advocate a contributory old age pension scheme. I am only reading from what I regard as the greatest authority in the world on this matter.
And a Scotsman at that.

And a Scotsman, such as my hon. friend praised the other day. I want to quote what he says about contributory schemes. He states:
In .passing it may be noted how the power of taxation has grown into a form of oppression beside which the modest efforts of the robber barons of the middle ages must appear crude.
And again:
Modern taxation is legalized robbery, and it is none the less robbery because it is effected through the medium of a political democracy which is made an accessory by giving it an insignificant share in the loot. But I do not think robbery is its primary object.
I will not read any more. I will conclude by saying that a contributory scheme of this kind, being compulsory, would mean confiscation. To my mind confiscation is to steal; to steal is to rob, and those who steal and rob are thieves and robbers. There is only one solution for the old age pension problem and that is the adoption of a philosophy which provides a national dividend as a right of citizenship. The Minister of Finance will make a name for himself in Canada-I suppose he has a name already; I think he is well respected in many quarters-he will move history and move this country if he adopts the principle that will make it possible to provide a national dividend, and he can get off to a good start with our aged mothers and fathers.

When a blind person marries another blind person his pension is reduced to $120. That seems hardly fair. In many cases a blind person needs someone else to look after him. I contend that the blind pension should be doubled in order to provide for this extra care which many blind persons need to help them out. Many accidents have occurred to blind persons because they tried to look after themselves. The government would be well advised to increase the blind pension. I was very much interested in what the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) said the other night, and I agree that the age limit should be reduced and the pension increased. The age limit should be reduced below twenty-one years, because there are many who have been blind from infancy.
I thought my hon. friend was advocating reducing the age limit for old age pensions to twenty-one years.
No; I am talking about blind pensions. Can the minister make a statement with regard to one blind person marrying another?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The pension is reduced to discourage the marriage of two blind persons.

To my way of thinking there is no^ old age pension scheme in Canada to-day. What we have is pauper's relief for those who are seventy years old and over, and are able to prove that they are absolutely destitute, and can produce -a birth certificate and other documents to prove their age and their economic position. I repeat; a citizen must be over seventy years of age and be absolutely destitute before he can qualify for this pauper's relief. In my opinion anyone who administers this pauper's relief as it stands in Canada to-day should hesitate
War Appropriation-Finance

before he speaks about it, because the results are a condemnation of any government and not a credit to a civilized people. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that a conscientious and self-respecting farmer treats his old horses better than we have treated our old worthy pioneers, the old age pensioners. What we need in Canada is a retirement allowance. No pauper's relief under the old patched-up legislation will do. The present act should be discarded and thrown in the waste-basket, and a more humane legislation should be passed.
I do not apologize for taking the time of the committee to speak on the problem of old age pensions. Several aspects of this problem have already been dealt with, but I wish to touch on some aspects which have been either inadequately dealt with or omitted altogether.
I suggest to the minister and the government that all citizens who no longer possess the power to earn a living should be automatically granted a retirement allowance adequate to provide them with a decent standard of living. If a Canadian citizen has lost his earning power he should be immediately granted a pension whether he is over sixty years of age or below sixty years of age. Those reaching the age of sixty who have not the power to earn for themselves a decent standard of living should be given a generous retirement allowance. The amount of the retirement allowance should be such that our . worthy pioneers could live in comfort and dignity. It could easily be fifty dollars a month for each individual pensioner.
Besides this regular monthly allowance our aged people should be provided with medical and dental care. Very few who have spoken in this debate so far have mentioned the importance of medical and dental care which our old people require. I suggest that the physical condition of each old age applicant be checked on applying for pension, and if medical or dental care is required money should lbe provided for it.
I am under the impression that Ontario grants medical care. I know that the old age pensioners have been getting it.
To my knowledge no province in Canada-

I am speaking from
knowledge. I know' that the old age pensioners in Ontario W'ere getting medical care, and they are still getting it unless a change has been made recently.
' Mr. LALONDE: It is the same in the province of Quebec, where the aged receive medical care from the health units.
Mr. HLYNIvA: If hon. members wrho have just interjected are ready to state that the

old age pensioners in Ontario and Quebec are receiving medical and dental care, and are provided with glasses when they require them and their teeth kept in proper condition, I will certainly be the first to express my appreciation of what has been done in that regard.

- I am speaking from knowledge w'hen I say that in Ontario the old age pensioners have been been receiving medical care, and are still receiving it unless some change has been made recently. I cannot speak definitely as to dental care.

I have received many
letters from old age pensioners across the country who have stated that they need money with w'hich to buy glasses because they can no longer read without them, and they need dental attention. That is why I have included this point in my notes, to bring it before the committee. There is no reason why this nation cannot provide our aged people with complete medical and dental care, provide them with glasses, dentures when they need them, and so forth.
Provision should also be made for funeral expenses of old age pensioners. As things stand to-day, the old age pensioner is forced to put away a few dollars from his .meagre twenty dollars a month pension so that he may be buried decently. This country could easily provide for funeral expenses, and let our worthy old pioneers enjoy the few dollars of pension they now receive.
I wish to say a few words on proof of age. I have many letters in my office from applicants who tried to get the old age pension but were turned down on the ground that they were unable to produce their birth certificates. I submit, Mr. -Chairman, that a great many of our citizens cannot produce their birth certificates. Many of them come from different European countries where the difficulty of getting birth certificates would be very great. But as the law now stands they .must be seventy years of age and produce their birth certificates before they are granted a pension. Surely it is too much to expect that every citizen treasure his birth certificate, keep it in a safe for years so that he can produce it when asked.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: They can make a Statutory declaration.

I know of many instances in which the old age pension authorities refused to accept a statutory declaration. The applicant is asked to go out and find someone who remembers the day when the applicant was born. That is pretty hard to do, and so I say provision should be made to relieve them of this requirement, particularly those

War Appropriation-Finance
who have come from European countries and whose birth certificates have been destroyed or lost. This is extremely important to many citizens in western Canada. Perhaps even some members of parliament could not find their birth certificates. Perhaps some of them would not want anyone to know when they were born, because the attitudue of some would indicate that their birth took place somewhere back in the seventeenth century; at lease one might assume that -when one hears them speak on measures which are urgently needed to-day.
Another suggestion I would make is that national registration should be used for the preparation of the lists of those qualifying for retiring allowance. Every citizen of Canada has certain obligations to Canada; he should also have certain privileges. If a young man is required for military service, under our laws he is called up, and he must obey the law or he is punished. My suggestion is that every Canadian be accorded similar privileges commensurate with his duties. When he becomes of pensionable age a notice should be sent to him to appear before the board to give a statement of his position. If his income is less than is required to provide a decent standard of living he should be immediately granted his allowance. If a citizen fails to accept his share of Canada's wealth and the heritage to which he is entitled he should be soundly scolded and told that unless he accepts his share it will be distributed among those who are kind enough to accept their cheques. That is the sort of attitude we should take. Again, every pensioner should be allowed to keep property up to a value of $3,500. Why not? He is not going to take it with him when he dies. But no; our present attitude is to grind him down and hold him to the ground to his last day. Surely we should be more human.
In a copy of the "Old Age Pensioner", a publication issued in British Columbia in the interest of old age pensioners, I notice these words:
Not only was it necessary to have an increase in the pension and reduction of the age limit, but something should surely be done to humanize the regulations and those who administer them. Too long had these worthy pioneers suffered by the indignities placed upon them and it was high time a halt was called.
These words were uttered by a gentleman interested in the subject of old age pensions, m asking the government to humanize the regulations and the handling of the whole problem.
Up until recently in my own constituency very few pensioners got as much as S20 a
month. Always there was some sort of deduction. An old mother is usually told to go and live with her daughter or her neighbours or someone else; and if she argues that the daughter has her own children to support and cannot provide her with living quarters, she is then told that she can do anything she wants and that that is the decision of the board and she will have to abide by it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, let me correct my hon. friend. The average pension paid in Alberta is $22.82.
I agree with the minister; with the assistance that the provincial government of Alberta has given to pensioners-
I thought it was $30.
-some of the pensioners can now receive as much as $30.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me correct my hon. friend. The average pension is $22.82 exclusive of the provincial supplement.

So much the better. But I never ran across anyone in my constituency until these changes were made who received $20 a month. I know what I am talking about. I have never met anyone in my constituency who received that much. There was always a deduction.
Did the hon. member say, hundreds of them?
Hundreds of them.

He must have a great old age
pensioner constituency.

Well, I have nearly fifty thousand people in my constituency. I know how anxious the minister and those who sit on the government side are to defend the present system, but let me tell them that these conditions have existed too long; it is about time that the regulations were humanized. I am glad to hear from the minister that the average pension, exclusive of provincial assistance, which is being paid in Alberta is $22.82. Any case which is referred to me in the future of old age pensioners who are not getting their share I intend to pass on to the minister, and I shall see how many of them are granted the amount to which they are entitled. It is all right to talk theoretically about these things, but in practice there is absolutely nothing to be proud of. I have had to go to the boards and try to rectify various cases, but I was told it is simply impossible to do anything because such were the regulations and th' / had to

iVnr Appropriation-Finance

abide by them. Naturally those who administer the regulations are in the driver's seat, and the old age pensioner is forced to accept what he is given.
I wish next to plead the case of those who do not speak adequately either the English or the French language. A large number of our Canadian pioneers in the west, particularly in the northern part of the prairie provinces, settled together in blocks. For many years there were no schools in the districts and they had no opportunity of learning the English language. To-day, if they have reached the age of seventy, they cannot obtain a pension because, they are told, "You must be a citizen; you must have your citizenship certificate." If these old folks apply for their citizenship certificates they are told to go home, that certificates will not be granted because they do not know the English language. Surely that is an unfair attitude to take. These people are pioneers; they have contributed much to the development of this country. Is there not at least one minister who would get up and say that now is the time to show our appreciation of what these people have done for this country, in which many of them have lived for fifty years or more? Yet two or three years ago they were celebrating their fiftieth anniversary of their coming to Canada, this very government failed even to send a government representative to their convention. That is not the attitude that makes for true Canadianism. That is not the attitude which should be adhered to. It is about time someone studied the problems of these people with a view to treating them as they should be treated.
I should like now to touch upon the subject discussed by the hon. member for Macleod, when he referred to the oft-repeated phrase, "something for nothing." A large number of members in the house object to that phrase because they would not want the people to know that they can get something to which they are entitled without working for it. Why should the people not be taught just the opposite? Why should they not be told that there is a certain heritage to which each citizen is entitled? That is the point of view we should all take. Certainly we should not raise our voices in ridicule when we speak of heritage. When an hon. member ridicules that expression, or ridicules us by reference to $25 a month, it immediately indicates a process of thinking that I could not possibly describe properly.
Reference has been made to contributory pensions. I suggest the reason why this government, or governments which have preceded it, have not brought in an adequate and

proper old age pension scheme or a proper scheme of retirement allowances, is that they did not want to stand in the way of insurance companies and, so that the companies could advertise in the press, and make use of pictures depicting misery, and say, "Unless you buy an endowment policy you will find yourself in a similar position."
That is the catch. I say the people of this nation should support the principle of insurance. They should be insured, but insurance should not stand in the way of the old age pensioner. And if we are going to have-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member is going pretty far. I do not think I can remember anyone having gone quite so far as that before to the length of saying that the reason the government is-not making a more generous provision for old age pensioners is that it is desirous of helping the insurance companies. I deny that, completely, both for myself and on behalf of the government, and I ask the hon. member to withdraw it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are discussing old age pensions. Surely hon. members should keep within the limit of the item. I have some responsibility in the matter and I must insist that this be done. I have ruled to that effect, and I repeat that hon. members must keep within the item before the committee.

I am not going to argue the point, but I must say that if we are to have a contributory pension scheme in Canada we shall undoubtedly have to compete with insurance companies. It will be a choice between one and the other. The point I wish to make is that if the government cannot give our citizens non-contributory old age pensions, the scheme will be of less value, because even as conditions are to-day our citizens can. insure on their own behalf. They can insure with one of the insurance companies, and be cared for when they reach the age of sixty years or over. As has been said so often by the hon. member for Lethbridge and other hon. members of this group, every citizen in this nation is entitled to a certain heritage-as a right of citizenship. A right to an old age pension is part of that heritage.
The minister said that I have gone beyond what he expected. However, I have noticed in the last four and a half years that unless one puts a problem straight to the government, the minister under whose jurisdiction the problem comes ignores the representations made, and that is the end of it. I would like the minister to read the letters I receive from old age pensioners. I would like him to read the letters which come from people who are

War Appropriation-Finance
either refused or receive pensions inadequate to care for them in the circumstances in which they find themselves. Therefore I do not apologize to the committee or to anyone else for urging as strongly as I can upon the government that something more be done with respect to old age pensions.

Mr. Chairman, I am not
going to apologize for making a few remarks on this subject. The only wonder to me is that such a debate as this is necessary in this day and age. I have wondered why there is any opposition or any hesitation on the part of members, or people outside the house. I wonder why there should be any longer any reluctance to pay a decent, civilized old age pension to citizens of Canada who are too old to work and who have failed to provide, as the saying goes, for a rainy day.
It seems to me the opposition springs from two points of view. There are those who still ask -where the money is to come from- although I think they are not in as large numbers as they were. The other kind of opposition comes from those who regard thrift, which in -their meaning is nothing but the saving of money, as the greatest of all virtues. From that they draw the conclusion that if an individual has not provided for his old age it proves that he has not led a good life, or even a useful one.
Mention has been made of the superiority of the Scot in the matter of thrift. I happened to be in Scotland last winter, and while there met a number of Scotsmen. During a discussion I was told that while the Scots were probably better thinkers than the English, the English had sounder instincts. That reminds me of a story of Doctor Johnson. While in the highlands he was told by some Scotch people, with great pride, that one could buy twenty eggs for a shilling. Doctor Johnson, with the sounder instinct of the English-if I may say so-replied at once, "The reason for that is not the plentiful supply of eggs, but the scarcity of pennies."
The statement has been made that a government can distribute to the people only what money has been previously contributed by them. I hold in my hand a book which was lately sent to me called " Monetary Experiment," by Richard A. Lester. Mr. Lester was born in New York stete, educated at Yale and Princeton. He holds the Ph.D. degree from Princeton. He has devoted his time to teaching. He was an instructor in economics at Princeton, assistant professor of economics at Haverford college, and is now assistant professor of economics at the university of Wash-
100-222 J
ington. For a time he was an analyst with the United States treasury. This book deals with experiments in money in the American colonies.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have no objection to hearing read a book written at that time, but I must remind the hon. member that we are now dealing with old age pensions. Surely this is not the time to deal with social theories and new economic problems or panaceas. I repeat that I must make a ruling at some time, and I would ask the hon. member to keep within the orbit of the item now before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to argue the point with you, but I want to read the quotation for this reason: the excuse that is given everywhere for the failure to pay more adequate pensions is, where is the money to come from? The statement has already been made in this committee that it is impossible for a government to distribute to a people money which has not already been surrendered to the government. Here is a matter of history. I wish to quote only a few lines, as follows:
When Maryland first issued paper money in 1733, most of it was given away-a certain sum to each inhabitant over fifteen years of age. This was done in order that the paper money might be "the more useful to the inhabitants" and its circulation made as "speedy and diffusive as .possible." The legislature hoped by this means "to remove the difficulties under which the inhabitants had long laboured." In a sense this "bounty" was a sort of "social dividend," similar to that advocated by Major Douglas in his books on social credit.
At the end of the chapter he sums up this particular experiment in these words:
From his detailed study of forty-five years of money in Maryland, Professor Gould concludes:
"Considering the peculiar benefits to grain and tobacco culture, the conveniences offered to trade, the exceptionally high exchange that the bills maintained throughout most of their life, and the faithful redemption of every shilling at face value, it is hardly too much to say that this was the most successful paper money issued by any of the colonies."
The author of the book, as I said, is a qualified economist who has held the position of analyst with the United States treasury. I do not think it is necessary to enlarge on the point as to where the money is to come from, because everybody has heard it said that if we can finance a war of course we can finance the peace.
But let us turn to the other objection to paying adequate pensions on a non-contributory basis. The idea seems to be, as expressed here, that you cannot get something for nothing; that in order to provide for old age every man should save money. I am going to make this statement to the committee: whenever a man
War Appropriation-Finance

or a citizen ceases to work-I do not care whether he has a million dollars saved up or not, it does not make any difference-he immediately ceases to contribute to the work or to the effort of the nation and he is bound to live on the bounty of the rest of the country. The idea that a man can save money and then at the end his life live off what he has saved and not at the expense of the community is, I am convinced, pure fallacy. I was reminded of this by a book which I read quite a few years ago and which I procured from the library this afternoon. It is called " Essays in Persuasion," by Maynard Keynes. In his chapter on inflation and deflation Mr. Keynes makes some remarks on the saving of money. He says:
There are to-day many well-wishers of their country who believe that the most useful thing which they and their neighbours can do to mend the situation is to save more than usual.
Of course, Keynes was writing during the depression, after the last war, in 1925, I think. The quotation continues: *
If they refrain from spending a larger .proportion of their incomes than usual they believe that they will have helped employment. Now, in certain circumstances all this would be quite right, but in present circumstances, unluckily it is quite wrong. It is utterly harmful and misguided-the very opposite of the truth; for the object of saving' is to release labour for employment on producing capital goods such as houses, factories, roads, machines and the like. But if there is a large unemployed surplus already available for such purposes, then *the effect of saving is merely to add to this surplus and therefore to increase the number of the unemployed. Moreover, when a man is thrown out of work in this or any other way, his diminished spending power causes further unemployment amongst those who would have produced what he can no longer afford to buy. and so the position gets worse and worse in a vicious circle.
The best guess I can make is that whenever you save five shillings, you put a man out of work for a day. Your saving that five shillings adds to unemployment to the extent of one man for one day-and so on in proportion. On the other hand, whenever you buy goods you increase employment-though they must be British, home-produced goods if you are to increase employment in this country. After all, this is only tile plainest common sense. For if you buy goods someone will have to make them. And if you do not buy goods the shops will not clear their stocks, they will not give repeat orders, and someone will be thrown out of work.
Those are the words of Maynard Keynes, who is reckoned one of the great economists; and they are in direct contradiction to the theories that are always advanced whenever the subject of old age pensions is brought up. The statement always is made that people are not entitled to pensions unless they have saved sufficient money to provide for their old age. And who is to value the contribution that any man may make during his life?

What about a mother who raises a large family of from six to a dozen children, whose husband earns barely enough to keep them, and certainly not enough to provide for any incidentals? Having raised her family; having done all the work for them and, as far as wages go, having received nothing for it; having put the welfare of her children before the accumulation of savings for her own old age, is she to be penalized because she has not saved sufficient money to provide for her needs? That is the position to-day. And I would ask this. In a country as empty as Canada, where we are bringing in Asiatics to fill up the waste spaces, what more valuable contribution could anyone make than by raising a family? Yet to-day the people are penalized for doing so. We all know what avarice does to a nation. We need only look at Roman history to learn that those people became so "thrifty" and so money-piinded that they could not even reproduce their own numbers, and so there came about the decline and fall of the Roman empire. So it is in Canada; we have pretty well reached the stage, outside the province of Quebec, when the people cannot afford to raise enough children to populate their own country.
What does the hon. member mean when he says we are bringing in Asiatics? We are not bringing in any now, are we?
They are refugees. I do not know where they come from; I cannot find out.
They are not Asiatics, are they?

I do not know where they come from, but we have brought in quite a number.
With regard to the future, we are told by the government and by other leaders that we must have a new order, a new world. When you boil down this new world it comes to this, as far as I can make out, that everybody is to be put to work. I do not think there is anything new about that; it seems to me the oldest thing in the world. I presume that if the work does not come about naturally then it will be created for its own sake. Let me put it from the point of view of providing employment for the majority of the people after the war. If you are going to have full production then you must have full consumption. There is no question about that; and if all the younger people are going to have full-time employment then the surplus must be distributed to those too old to work. If there is to be any involuntary unemployment

War Appropriation-Finance
after the war-and I have not met anyone yet who does not fear it-surely that unemployment should fall upon those who are old and not upon those in the prime of life.
So I say that from every point of view you wish to look at it, whether from the moral or the practical, there is everything to be said for properly looking after our old people. I know that what is good in war is not necessarily good in peace. As someone has said, war is hell, and we do not want to carry the conditions of war into the time of peace. But if we are to prepare for the new age that we hear about in this chamber and elsewhere, a very good way to begin, and a proof of the earnestness of those who talk about it, would be a guarantee to those who are too old to work, those who have done their share of work in this country, that henceforth they shall be granted more than the bare necessities of life-at times they do not even get that- and that in future they may enjoy some of the comforts as well, whether or not they have accumulated savings deposits of money. Again I ask, who is to judge the value of any man's contribution? Who is to value the life work of any man or any woman? Certainly it cannot be done by the size of his or her bank balance.

I am sure there is not an hon. member in this chamber who could not speak on old age pensions and pensions to the blind for at least forty minutes. But when I remember that the minister is to bring down his budget next week, or at least very soon; when I remember that we have been discussing this matter for two days, I feel that if I spoke for forty minutes now, or for five minutes, I would be committing an unpardonable sin. I know we have much to say, but I think the patience of the committee has been exhausted. I believe we should call a halt to this discussion and say, "Carried."

I would have felt the same way as the hon. member for Fort William, but if we can spend practically half a day on strawberries, an hour and a half on empty beer bottles, quite a while on dressed and undressed poultry, and so on, surely we can spare some time for the aged people. I do not want to quote from any books or deliver a full thesis on the question of the aged. I believe everyone here could approach the problem from the humanitarian point of view. Among the saddest scenes I have to witness is old men and women selling newspapers in the city of Montreal on cold winter nights. Often I say to myself there must be something radically wrong with this world of ours that such things should have to be. Each of us is confronted
with such a scene now and then, and I am sure we all feel the same way. I do believe, however, that in dealing with the problems of the aged it is. hardly proper for an hon. member of this house to slur our Asiatic allies or anyone else, or to go in for racialism, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin did.
Not at all; I maintain that charity begins at home.
Our Chinese allies have been fighting our battles for many years; they are a very fine people. The Siberian corps at Stalingrad were very fine people too.
That is all right, but charity still begins at home.

So far as we are concerned I should say the word "Asiatics" was used by the hon. member in a racial sense and in a manner unbecoming to any hon. member of this house. What was the obstacle placed in the way of the payment of old age pensions in Canada? At one time it was the province of Quebec. I can remember not so many years ago when the leaders of the government in Quebec used to say, "We do not want any old age pensions in this province because it will destroy charity." Others used to say that it would take away the responsibility of children to look after their parents. I would say that those people were hypocrites. They did not mean anything of the kind; they were just thinking of the money that would have to be paid out of the provincial treasury.
I am glad that to-day the province of Quebec has taken the lead in asking that .the age limit be reduced to sixty-five years, and the government of that province deserves congratulations. One of the obstacles of olden days is now out of the way. Why should it not be possible to speed up the dominion-provincial conference in order that this matter may be settled as soon as possible? These old people cannot wait. Many of them feel that they never know how many more years of life they have. I wrent through an election campaign not so long ago and many of them came to me and asked, "What will you do about it?" I told them I would do my best. They cannot wait; they feel that their years are numbered.
This matter should not be postponed too long. I understood that the dominion-provincial conference was to take place in the early summer, and this problem of old age pensions should be on the agenda. This government is considering the payment of family allowances and I think that problem and the problem of old age pensions can be considered together. In both cases the people concerned are helpless; they need someone to
War Appropriation-Finance

look after them, and considered from this point of view we should not let down our old people.
I remember back in the days of unemployment when the labour leaders used to say that the age limit should be reduced to sixty years in order to provide more jobs for younger people. Many thousands of young men will be coming back after the war and if these older people could step aside it would provide many jobs for them. This matter should be considered as a post-war problem. Whether the scheme is to be contributory or noncontributory, I believe the people of Canada will not quarrel about it once they feel assured that they will receive an old age pension when they reach the age of sixty or perhaps sixty-five years.
Many hon. members have given credit to the trade union movement for the improvement in old age pensions. I was especially gratified to hear the Minister of Labour give credit to the trade union movement and the work they have done for the aged. In a memorandum submitted to the Prime Minister and members of the dominion government by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on Friday, February 25, 1944, it is stated:
While some adjustments have been made in regard to pensions .paid to aged people and the blind, in our opinion the adjustments were not sufficient to meet the increase in cost of living and some further adjustments should be made immediately. Some of the provinces have taken action in this regard but we would_ suggest that your government take the lead in calling a conference of all the provinces in order to establish once for all an adequate pension on a uniform scale that aged and incapacitated persons may enjoy a full life.
That is a very moderate demand on the part of the trade union movement and it should receive the full support of this committee.
Before sitting down I should like to say a few words in support of those who are not citizens of this country. I have had people come to me and explain how they have put off becoming citizens, and now they find themselves too old. Quite often they do not speak the language very well and because of their experience with police in their homeland they are fearful of going down to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They have many other reasons for not becoming citizens. The result is that they cannot get pensions. Many of these people have lived and worked in this country for a number of years, and they should be able to enjoy the few years that remain to them without being punished for not having become citizens. Whether they have their papers or not, they are just as loyal as anybody else.

All hon. members, no matter
where they sit, are in favour of increasing pensions for our aged people and decreasing the age limit. The records of the house over the past years show that I along with other members have championed the cause of old age pensions. I think, however, it ill behooved the hon. member who has just taken his seat to accuse other hon. members of taking up time, in speaking about strawberries. Although strawberries may have nothing to do with old age pensions, I, as one of those who did speak about strawberries, have no apology to make for having done so.
There was a principle at stake in that, connection, as there is a principle at stake here to-day. In that case we had a board appointed by the government fixing prices and the only court of appeal to which we had access was this House of Commons. Having appealed *to the board and having received no redress from the board, we then brought the matter, as was our right, to the House of Commons. That was the reason why many of us entered into that discussion and took up the time of the house. on that occasion, and it ill behooves the hon. member for Cartier to chide any hon. member of the house for doing that.
I sat in my place and listened to him take up about forty minutes in discussing a man by the name of Kirkconnell. Those who live in glass-houses should not throw stones, and this place has more windows than any other place I know of which are easily broken if a man begins to throw stones. Reference has been made by the hon. member to Asiatics, but may I say that at any time if I referred to Asiatics I did so in a fair way. I have never attempted to raise racial hatred. Although I well remember when, in 1934, the Japanese were being discussed, hon. members belonging to his party used that old tirade, or old argument of their's by saying that I was doing it just to draw a red herring across the trail. I have always approached the question from the practical point of view and with no idea of causing racial hatred.
I rose, however, on this occasion to add my voice to those who have spoken on this question of old age pensions which is one that should not be allowed to die down. Time has moved on, and we have reached the stage when the old people in this country should get a better deal than parliament has granted them up to the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I .suppose I should answer
some of the questions that have been asked and deal with the matter as a whole for perhaps fifteen or twenty minutes. I did not make any general remarks when introducing

IFar Appropriation-Finance
this item to the committee. Perhaps I should have done so. Perhaps I would have done so had I known the debate would be so protracted.
At the present time we have an old age pension system in Canada which is far from satisfactory. It is far from satisfactory mainly because of the division of responsibility between the dominion parliament and the legislatures of the provinces. I have never disguised the fact that this system is an unsatisfactory one. Those of us who have any responsibility for its administration see evidence of that every day. For that reason I have been saying, for the last year or two at least, that I hope to see the time, and I hope it will be at an early date, when we shall have a satisfactory system of old age pensions in Canada under one jurisdiction, where the pension will be more generous and where it will be payable at an earlier age than at present,
And be more uniform.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; if it is under one jurisdiction it will be uniform. But we cannot move from our present divided jurisdiction system into that better system without a transfer of certain jurisdiction from the provinces to the dominion. That certainly is true if we adopt the contributory system of old age pensions. I have not had experience, as members of the house have pointed out, in the administration of social service legislation; and if the dominion government undertakes the administration of a federal pension scheme, I am inclined to agree that its administration should not be in the Department of Finance. 1 do not say that because I admit a hard and unsympathetic heart. I say that because I think it could be more appropriately administered by a department of social welfare than by the Department of Finance. The reason why the administration of the old age pension scheme, in so far as it is administered by the dominion government, is in the Department of Finance is that we are merely contributors to nine provincial old age pension systems, and that is a fact which so many members lose sight of entirely. The payment of old age pensions from the beginning has been regarded as primarily the responsibility of the provinces, just like the payment of mothers' allowances, just like the administration of workmen's compensation. It is a scheme to which we contribute, and which is administered by the provinces. It is administered by regulations agreed upon by the provinces and the dominion. There is a dominion Old Age Pensions Act which authorizes us to contribute.
In the early days of the old age pensions legislation the federal contribution was fifty per cent of the pension. Shortly after 1930 that was increased to seventy-five per cent of the pension, and it became more unsatisfactory from our point of view. I do not mean because it cost us more than it would have had our contribution remained at fifty per cent, but it became a case where the administrative authority was less concerned about the matter .because the paying authority was to the extent of seventy-five per cent of the pension another authority altogether.
Accordingly that system went on, a most unsatisfactory system; I do not deny that at all. I want to see it move into a more modern, more advanced and more generous system than the system we have at the present time. The only way we can do that sensibly is, I think, by adopting a contributory system which will be administered entirely by the dominion government. That would probably cost the dominion treasury more than the present system, even though it is a contributory system, because it is not true to say, as some members have said, that under a contributory system everything is paid for by the contributors. A large part is paid by the state. The only way in which we could get a transfer of jurisdiction would be by an amendment to the British North America Act. Whether we can get the provinces to agree to that I do not know, and whether the people will accept a system of contribution I do not know.
Has the matter been discussed with the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; that is a matter which will have to be taken up and will be taken up at the approaching provincial conference. We have come out in the speech from the throne in favour of a contributory sysem. Whether it can be done or not I do not know. I have listened to members and most of them talk as if it were wrong to ask anybody to contribute. Perhaps I am not qualified by experience to argue the matter thoroughly, but students of these questions, experts on these problems, all seem to agree-there seems to be complete unanimity-that the sounder .system is the contributory one. Sir William Beveridge says so; Marsh, who wrote the report to which the hon. member for Vancouver South referred, says so. They have a contributory system in the country which is always quoted by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as the most advanced country in the world, namely, New Zealand, where they contribute to their social security measures. I think it is a sounder system. I think people ought to contribute. Remember, in
War Appropriation-Finance

unemployment insurance we do not say that the workman should not contribute to the fund out of which he gets benefits when he is unemployed. We do not think there that an outright dole is better than the insurance principle.
It works out in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They contribute, and there are very sound reasons for a contributory system. However, that is in the future. In the meantime we have the present system to administer.
What is the situation? We started out in the beginning with a maximum pension of S20 a month. In the early part of 1941 a cost-of-living bonus was being paid to persons engaged in industry, and .there was a great demand that we pay the cost-of-living bonus to old age pensioners or do something along that line. In November, 1941, I announced the government's policy to the. house. I stuck to the principle that has always been preserved in this pension scheme, namely, that it was primarily a matter of provincial responsibility; I said that if any province wished to pay a supplemental allowance we would alter the regulations in such a way that they could do so without that supplemental allowance being regarded as income, and certain provinces did that.
Prior to the passing of the order in council of last year six provinces had made provision for a supplemental allowance: British Columbia, $5 to each pensioner from April 1, 1942; Alberta, $5 to each pensioner from April 1, 1942, plus up to an amount of $5 where income is less than $365 a year; Manitoba, $1.25 to each pensioner from January 1, 1943; Saskatchewan $1.25 to each pensioner from January 1, 1943; Ontario, 15 per cent of pension payable under the act from July 1, 1943; Nova Scotia, $10 a month payable at the discretion of the pension authority to pensioners with income of less than $365 a year, from June 1, 1943. That provision made in the various provinces is illuminating. It shows the different views which the different provincial authorities took with respect to adding to the pension by way of supplemental allowance.
As a result of that and the addition to the pension which we provided last summer, the maximum payments per month now allowed in the various provinces are: Alberta, $30, plus $5 per year; British Columbia, $30; Manitoba, $25; New Brunswick, $25; Nova Scotia, $30; Ontario, $28; Prince Edward Island, $25; Quebec, $25; Saskatchewan, $25. If hon. members are interested in the average paid in each province apart from the supplemental

allowances, I can give the figures as of March 31 last: Alberta, $22.82; British Columbia, $23.55; Manitoba, $23.41; New Brunswick, $17.69; Nova Scotia, $18.06; Ontario, $23.09; Prince Edward Island, $18.53; Quebec, $22.54; Saskatchewan, $23; Northwest Territories, $24.55.
In November or December, 1941-whenever it was that I announced the government's policy-I also said that if all or substantially all the provinces wished us to agree to increase the maximum amount of pension payable we would give attention to doing that; and the provinces, somewhat slowly, began over the next year or year and a half to make requests that that be done. The last of -these requests was received in July, 1943, and we passed an order in council increasing the maximum from $20 to $25 a month. There is some demand at the present time that the age be reduced from seventy to sixty-five years, and the decision of the government has been that they should pursue exactly the same course as they did with regard to the raising of the maximum payable, namely, that they should not attempt to force this on the provinces, it being primarily a provincial responsibility; that they should say to the provinces, as I said to the provinces the other day in the statement I made in this house, that if all or substantially all the provinces should make representations to the dominion government in favour of a reduction of the eligible age from seventy to sixty-five years the government would give consideration to those representations. That is just as I did before; and I do not think, if we are to keep our policy consistent, if we are to pursue a policy which will have regard to the position and rights of the provincial authorities and respect the provincial jurisdiction, we can do anything but that.

speechtext: Has there been any reaction from a-ny province yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not since I made the statement the other day; but three or four provinces had indicated -previously that they would like to have the ages reduced-one of the provinces, I think to sixty years. But the position we felt we should take was very carefully thought out.
