speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I believe certain provinces are requesting an increase in the amount. The provinces contribute only twenty-five per cent to all this, and .requests come forward with considerable facility. In a good many cases they do not need very much encouragement. But that is the situation.
As I say, I think this is a reasonable course to pursue under the present system, the system of divided jurisdiction which we have had established here since 1926. Not only is it consistent but it is, I believe, the correct and proper course to pursue.
After we passed the order in council of last summer raising the maximum amount from $20 to $25, the question arose as to whether the permissible outside income should not be raised to $425. One or perhaps more than one of the provinces had asked that at the beginning, I remember particularly the province of Manitoba. They thought the matter through and coupled their request with a request for an increase in the maximum amount payable. But most of the provinces said nothing about that; the question was not discussed; and I did not feel free on a basis of general provincial consent to take that step, because it would be not only increasing the amount payable to existing pensioners but enlarging the class of pensioners, and would raise administrative burdens for the provinces as well as cast further expense on them. That was taken up later with the provinces by the dominion, and the other day, this order in council, which in a sense is consequential to the order in council of last summer, was passed having effect from April 1 or such later date as the province in any particular case might desire.
It has been suggested by one of the speakers that we should put these changes we have made into legislation, that we should amend the act.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I do not like the
act as it stands well enough to bring in amending legislation if we can help it. If we are to legislate on the subject of old age pensions, I should like to put something on the statute books more satisfactory than a patched-up 1926 Old Age Pensions Act; and I think, if there is patching-up to be done, it should be done by order in council.
Hon. gentlemen may be afraid that the authority for the orders in council will run out before there is a chance for legislation. Let me point out that the War Measures Act of the last war ran until some time in 1920-* I have not the exact date-and there is no prospect of the present War Measures Act
losing its effect for a very considerable length of time to come. It does not pass out at the end of the war or six months after; it passes out when the necessity for it, in the opinion of the government of the day, no longer exists.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Or when the courts say the necessity for it no longer exists?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think so. My hon. friend suggests that it is perhaps when the courts say the necessity for it no longer exists, but certainly there is a post-war period during which the War Measures Act will be in force, and I suggest that there is plenty of time for legislation such as this, and that we should not enact legislation for old age pensions until we have a more satisfactory system, jurisdictionally and otherwise, than we have at the present time.
Certain specific suggestions have been made during the course of the debate, and I will try to deal with a few of them. I cannot make any definite pronouncements on the suggestions which have been made, but in certain cases at least I am prepared to give them consideration.
One was that no rental should be charged up against the occupant of premises which he owns. Rental is charged up against them at the present time because of a regulation which was agreed upon by the provinces and the dominion, and I assume that that regulation was based upon the desirability of eliminating discrimination between pensioners who occupied their own property and those who roomed, or something of that kind.
Those who had to pay rent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One must be very careful in changing these regulations not to give rise to discrimination, because nothing creates a sense of injustice so much as discrimination.
The home owner has to pay taxes.
Well, the roomer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but that is not equivalent. Taxes are merely a fraction of the occupancy value of the premises.
Another suggestion was with regard to dependents' allowance and assigned pay, and I should like to review that story. In the first place let us take the case of the person to whom the soldier assigns pay, there being no dependents' allowance. In that case it was considered, first, that it must be regarded as income. Then a great many cases came to the attention of the pension authorities in

War Appropriation-Finance

which these seemed to be the facts: it was found that in many cases pay was being assigned to persons who held the pay in trust for the assignors. That was particularly true in cases where there was no dependents' allowance. It was true in cases where there was no condition of dependency. So that it became impossible for the authorities to decide as to whether the assignee held the amount in trust for the assignor, or otherwise; and it was decided, therefore, in those cases to wipe it out as income altogether, and to consider it the property of the assignor, and not to consider it the income of the assignee.
The next case about which complaint is made in the house by a great many members is the one where there is no question of dependency, because dependents' allowance is being paid. It was considered that under the regulations, there being no question of dependency, the dependents' allowance board having decided that the assignee is a dependent of the assignor, in that case what the assignee received by way of dependents' allowance and assigned pay must be regarded as income. The result was that the old age pensions in some cases were cut out or reduced.
I am not just sure what the suggestions are that have been made in this debate, but I gathered from a remark made by one of the members that he thought possibly one should be considered as income, but not the other. Someone asked the question whether both were regarded as income. There is some argument for giving assigned pay the same treatment in a case where there is dependents' allowance as in a case where there is no dependents' allowance. There is some argument for that. But there is also some argument on the other side, too. All I can say about it is that I took to heart what some members said about this situation. It may be a little difficult to explain, and it may be thought there should not be strictness in adherence to the regulations. I would be prepared to give consideration to the suggestions which have been made, and see whether they can be squared with the regulations or, if not, whether the regulations should in some way be limited. But that would be a matter of agreement with all the provinces, as I have said before.
I wish to point out at once that if we build up too much the income of the mother of a member of the services, in proportion to the income of the mother of someone who is not a member of the services, but living next door, the latter-mentioned mother will say there is discrimination.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not in the case of assigned pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps not in the case of assigned pay. But if dependents' allowance were allowed to go you would have a lot of difference in the treatment of two old age pensioners who might be living side by side. That must always be considered when one considers amending regulations.
The hon. member for Macleod asked a specific question regarding to what property of the pensioner a lien attaches. That is a matter of provincial legislation. I presume the regulations in the various provinces are different. No lien is created by dominion legislation. The lien has to be created by provincial legislation, and they can make the lien attach to any property they wish. The most common provision is that it is a lien against the real or personal property of the pensioner.
Could a province waive that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes, they can do that. I believe the dominion act says it is a debt, does it not?
All the provinces have liens, have they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, they all have liens, but they do not necessarily all have the same kind.
None of them exercise them, do they?
Yes, they do.
British Columbia does not.
The dominion gets the blame for the property clause.
I thought it was the other way around.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Five of them do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The relative provision of the dominion legislation creates a debt, but it does not create a lien. The lien is created by the province.
It is a crown debt, and it is ahead of ordinary debts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
Oh, yes; a crown debt is ahead of my debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The income tax people do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a long story.

speechtext:
I would remind the minister that his parliamentary assistant has already made that point clear. He referred

TFar Appropnation-Finance
to it on March 23, when the house was told in answer to a question of mine that it is now up to each province whether the crown files liens, at least up to a certain value.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And according to subsequent information given in answer to a question, it now appears that British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia do not file liens up to the specified amount, which seems to leave it that the other four provinces do still avail themselves of that privilege.

Mr. Speaker-
Has the minister finished?

speechtext: I am afraid I have stirred this up, all over again. We could go on all afternoon and evening. I shall have to answer new questions that are asked.
I understand that the minister says he is in favour of having an amendment to the British North America Act to give the dominion exclusive jurisdiction over contributory old age pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

Does he mean that to include old age pensions to the people who would not be able to contribute to such a scheme? In other words, would the contributory scheme include all the persons who are now pensioners, or would it not? I do not know whether he thinks they, too, should come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly think they should. I think the dominion should have jurisdiction over the whole thing. The object would be eventually to work into a contributory scheme which would have very wide coverage. Of course it would not be contributory as far as present old age pensioners are concerned, because it is too late.
If the dominion takes over contributory old age pensions it should also take over present old age pensioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In some modified form, perhaps. But I would be in favour of the dominion dealing with old age pensions as a whole, because I do not think we can have a federal scheme and provincial schemes. We would just have confusion worse confounded.
Take over everything.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister did not stick to it.

The minister has repeated
this afternoon that old age pensions are in the same category as mothers' allowances and workmen's compensation. I wish he would go a little farther in his explanation of that statement, because actually the fact is that mothers' allowances and workmen's compensation are handled exclusively by the provinces. The dominion has nothing whatever to do with them and has never had. On the other hand, the dominion stepped in and passed the first Old Age Pensions Act and, as the minister said, is now paying three-quarters of the cost. Will he explain how he puts these three types of assistance on the same basis and then says that they are a provincial responsibility in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have explained that repeatedly in other years. The dominion did what it did in 1926 in order to get the provinces going; that was why. The provinces got under way under their own steam in the matter of mothers' allowances and workmen's compensation, but they were not getting ahead with old age pensions. Therefore the dominion adopted the principle of paying part of the cost which we have all repeatedly said we do not like, just for the sake of getting the provinces going.
Would the minister in his scheme suggest that the provinces be relieved of all costs, administrative and otherwise, if they transferred their jurisdiction to the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I would; but I wish to point out that that will be a big burden
War Appropriation-Finance

for the dominion to assume and it is tied up with financial adjustments and division of revenue fields and so forth with the provinces.
You will have to ask them to give up something else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know who will do
the giving up. The two things are tied up to one another.
No doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have a fairly satisfactory arrangement with regard to taxation fields for the w-ar period, but it- expires at the end of the war, and we shall have to get our minds down eventually to the question as to what taxes may be imposed by what authority.

This act was, in the first place, dominion legislation. By that I mean that the first statute with regard to old age pensions was a dominion statute. I remember the day when the Hon. Peter Heenan, then Minister of Labour, went to Toronto to have the agreement signed with the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, then premier of Ontario. Afterwards agreements were signed with the other provinces, and at the present time there is an old age pension scheme in every province.
The act was passed at a time when provincial rights were respected. It was not long after a judgment of the supreme court that was not appealed from by the government of the day, in which the respective powers of the dominion and the provinces were clearly stated. It is important to .note that it was the then Minister of Labour who went to Toronto to sign the agreement with the premier of Ontario; it was not the Minister of Finance of the day. I do not know whether or not since that time pensions have been placed under the Minister of Finance. Perhaps they have been, but they were not at the time. The idea of putting the plan on a fifty-fifty basis with the provinces was precisely to respect provincial autonomy. The provinces were told that the dominion had passed legislation in virtue of which a subsidy of fifty per cent would be paid to the provinces if they agreed to it, and it was up to them to establish an old age pension scheme within their boundaries.
It took some time to have this scheme accepted by all the provinces, but finally it was. Then Mr. Bennett came into powers He also respected provincial autonomy, but increased the dominion contribution by twenty-five per cent, making it seventy-five per cent. What people do not understand is that the dominion is paying seventy-five per cent and the prov-

inces only twenty-five per cent. They admin- _ ister the whole thing. The dominion has no responsibility to the people with regard to the administration of the scheme, but on the other hand all the blame is put on the dominion by the provinces when a pension is refused. The provinces say the regulations that have been passed by Ottawa prevent us from granting a pension, and so on. That is the story. This is most unsatisfactory legislation.
I will tell you, Mr. Chairman, what I think of old age pensions. I think it is a good thing.
I congratulate the minister for having raised the contribution from S20 to S25 a month.
It was a good step, but the age should be lowered to at least sixty-five years for the old and in so far as the blind are concerned, as soon as a child is acknowledged by the doctor to be blind he should be entitled to a pension if his parents have not sufficient means to pay for his care. Distinction should be made between those who have some means and those who have none. We now come to a basis of contribution. I will not discuss the question of contribution at all. How is it possible for a man who has nothing, who is destitute, to pay a contribution toward old age pension? Those who have sufficient means may buy an annuity from the Department of Labour. It still exists. It does not come under the Department of Finance unless things have been changed. We are not fighting here the case of those who have a sufficient income on which to live or who have independent means. We are fighting the case of the poor who have not the means to pay a contribution, who are destitute and who must not be left on the street. They are old. They have rendered a certain service to the community and they deserve some help from the state. That is the purpose of the old age pension, as explained by the legislators and by the members of the government of the day when this act was passed. It is easy to see in the speeches made at that time by the present Prime Minister and the Hon. Peter Heenan who was then Minister of Labour that the purpose of the old age pension was to help those who had no means on which to live and who were destitute, who had no children who could help them.
There is another matter I should like to mention. To-day a twenty-dollar bill does not go any farther than a ten-dollar bill used to go. These people have expenses to meet. Even those who have not much to live on have to pay more for their food, clothes and so on. Therefore they need a certain increase. [DOT] It is a matter that the minister has understood and I congratulate him upon having done so.
It is essential for the government to understand that discrimination exists when men

Private Bills
aged sixty-five do not get their pensions. How many suffer from rheumatism and are unable to work when they reach sixty, labourers, who did not save any money for their older days? I leave this to the minister's consideration. I hope he will realize the fact that the suggestion is unanimous; it has been made by all parties of the house.
There is perhaps this controversial question of dominion and provincial rights. The minister holds the view that this matter of old age pension should be under one jurisdiction. He is perfectly right. I agree with him; but we should not forget that taxation from which this old age pension is paid comes from the pocket of the Canadian taxpayer. The only question that arises as between a provincial payment and a dominion subsidy to the provinces is that of control. The taxpayer pays the same amount for the same purpose, but the question is whether the money is to be raised and controlled by the province or by the dominion. If the only purpose of the dominion government in establishing old age pensions was to see to it that the scheme was adopted by all the provinces, now that it has been so adopted; now that it is in force; now that it cannot be changed, surely that purpose has been realized.
How would it be possible to have the matter under one jurisdiction, which it is a desirable thing? It could be done by the Minister of Finance releasing a part of the taxation that formerly belonged to the provinces, to enable them to carry on the old age pension scheme. It is the easiest thing in the world. Take the succession duties, and things like that; if the minister would release the dominion succession tax and negotiate agreements under which the provinces would bind themselves to lower the age at which people could receive pensions, surely an agreement of that kind could be relied upon just as much as a treaty with a foreign nation. Why should provinces not be considered on the same footing as other countries? They are our own people; yet such a fuss is made when agreements are to be signed with the provinces. The time has come when our own people, the provinces of this country, should have priority over all other nations in their dealings with the dominion government. They are our own people; it is only natural that we,should look after them; so why not do it in an orderly way? Some people in the Department of Finance like complicated matters; instead of simplifying the procedure and allowing the provinces to be masters of their own destiny they say, "Well, we will get the money and we will give it back to you." What is the reason for that transaction? Why keep accountants
to write down the amount of money received
on behalf of the provinces and the amount of money that is returned to the provinces?
In a nutshell what I have to suggest to the minister is this: reduce the age at which the blind may receive pensions, so that they may be paid even to infants and children whose blindness is certified by competent doctors; lower to sixty-five the age at which old people may receive pensions; give pensions only to those who need them, but give pensions to all who need them. Then start once more to respect provincial autonomy. Give the provinces an opportunity to collect the amounts of money they collected previously, so that this scheme may be operated by the provinces themselves to the great benefit of all concerned.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the evidence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Old age pensions and pensions to the blind, $6,942,250.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not long detain the committee. I listened with interest this afternoon to the explanations of the minister, more especially as regards the trouble he was encountering in dealing with this subject, which is under dual jurisdiction. He also stated that he personally was in favour, later on possibly, of a contributory scheme, that he would be in favour of it if the provinces would agree. I do not think there will be much trouble in the provinces agreeing. If you go to a man and ask him to pay his debts he may quibble; but if you offer to pay half his debts you are much more likely to get a favourable response. If you go to him and offer to pay the whole bill, I do not think there would be a great deal of trouble in getting his consent. The

War Appropriation-Finance
trouble in 1926 and 1927 was that while we fully recognized, as we do still, that it was the obligation of the provinces, we could not make the provinces recognize their obligations, or at all events they would not do anything about them. The only way we could get action was not by waiting, dallying along the primrose path, but by taking action ourselves, and so we drafted a bill and passed it and said: This we will do, and you can come in or stay out. British Columbia immediately came in, and the other provinces one by one followed suit.
The outstanding feature on which the minister has not been able to meet the representations made to him the other day was as to reducing the age limit. I think he might have given a lead to the provinces in this matter. Nothing is to be gained by waiting on the provinces, with the provinces waiting on somebody else, but just as when we passed an act and said to the provinces, "We will contribute fifty per cent" we got action because the people of the provinces stirred up their governments, so that I think in this case the Minister of Finance might give the provinces another lead by proposing to reduce the age limit. I think he said that three or four provinces were already agreeable to that.
When I was discussing old age pensions the other night I raised two points. One was the danger of losing the last five dollars that was added to the pension last year. I find that the Minister of Finance admitted last year, as he did again this afternoon, that the increase then put on would be liable to be taken off if legislative action was not taken at the end of the war or in the meantime. I foresaw the danger of putting this in as a sort of cost of living bonus item which would disappear with the disappearance of the War Measures Act. But now the minister says that the War Measures Act of 1914 lasted for some years after the end of the last war. Although I cannot find any record of that, I take his word for it. Then he said that there was no hurry, that no doubt the War Measures Act would extend beyond the end of this war and there was time to deal with any emergency at that time. I do not just see the point. This is not like an act. This has not been done bv passing an act or by passing an order in council under the War Measures Act but merely by putting an item in the estimates which is contained in certain appropriations to be passed under the War Measures Act. Last year the minister simply rose in his place and did not consider it necessary even to put an item in the war appropriation. He simply said: We will take the necessary sum out of the war appropriation. There is no
guarantee that he will do so this year. We have confidence in him, of course, but there is no obligation on him to do so. After the war other governments, with other minds, may come into power and may say: We will drop this; we have r.o authority to pass further items of this sort under the War Measures Act. They might even go further if challenged and , say: It is obvious that the government that passed it did not intend it to be anything more than a temporary measure because they did not pass an act but simply put an item in the estimates, so that eventually it was nothing more than a temporary measure, a cost of living bonus, so to speak, which might be taken away. They would have a good argument in saying that.
The minister said that he did not like the act. But if we never voted for anything we did not like, sometimes governments would find their tenure of power somewhat slim. I think, with all deference to the minister, that was a weak argument. After all, it is only a small act and only a small amendment is required. If later on another act is necessary to bring in the contributory system the amendment would disappear with the disappearance of the act. Is there any harm in tying it up for the present in such a way that it will not disappear? Another, perhaps unsympathetic government might fall back on the contention that this was a temporary thing on account of war conditions and so on. I cannot see how my suggestion would do any harm; it would relieve these old people from the fear hanging over them that, for some minister's convenience in years to come, he might say, "Oh, times have changed; I am not going to put it in; what are you going to do about it?" We could do nothing about it; we could not point to a definite measure, unless passed the way I suggest. Therefore I urge that it would be a good thing to allow this simple matter to be inserted in the act itself.
If I were the leader of the party to my left I think I would be inclined to insist upon that, because I am sure it has the approval of the people as a whole. I would be inclined to say, "Well you have brought this in; you admit it is right; the people think it is right; you will put it in the act-or else". But of course that is for somebody else's judgment.
The second matter I brought up when I was speaking the other day-the minister did not allude to it-was that he should send this bill, and the regulations connected with it, which are the greatest source of trouble, to the committee appointed to deal with just such things; I mean the committee on industrial and international relations. It was dealt with on four different occasions, each time with
War Appropriation-Finance

some measure of profit, and out of the last discussion, came the bill itself. There are a number of small matters which we have not time to thresh out here, nor is a committee of 245 members adapted to discuss them, but they could well be discussed in the committee to which I have referred.
I mention only one or two points, although I could cite half a dozen or more. Take the one which says that a poor old man may have 160 acres of wild bush land, not worth the paper that the title is written on, but it is assessed at, we will say, $1,000 and he has to pay $20 a year taxes on it. The pension board say, "You own that property, it is assessed for $1,000; therefore, we say you have an income from that useless land of $50 a year and we take that off the amount of pension you have been getting". On top of that his taxes are $20, so that he is "out" $70 a year on some land of which he long since got tired, and which never did have any value except in some optimistic hope twenty or thirty years ago. It may be said that he could sell it and get rid of it. But it is the sort of thing you cannot sell. I made written application to the government, signed by an old age pension applicant, who stated, "I hereby convey and grant all my right, title and interest in such a piece of land to the government." But the government were too smart They would not take it. They said, "Not for us; we know better than that, and we don't want it." The alternative was to let it go to tax sale, we were told, and he could thus get rid of it. But no; first, it would take two or three years to get rid of it in that way. There were hard times during the depression; perhaps an election was coming on, and the government did not hold tax sales, so that the wretched man could not let it go to a tax sale, since none was being held, and he was caught between the two dilemmas. He could not get out of it at all. He could not sell it; he could not give it to the government, and he could not let it go to the tax sale. Things like that are well worth consideration by the committee.
They are charged five per cent on land which is not producing anything. That charge should be abolished.
The other point to which I particularly wish to refer is the assessment of the land. We got the regulations changed so that it would not read, as at first, the assessed value, but would read, the assessed value or the market value, whichever was deemed to be the more equitable. I immediately jumped at that concession and said to myself, now we shall be able to get a pension for that man or woman, because the market value of the

land is eighty cents and the assessed value is about $2,000. But the authorities would not do that, and said so. They told me, "We have the option." "No", I said, "the only option you have is to say which is the more equitable". They said, "It will save us trouble; we prefer to take the view that the assessors are men of ability and assess the land properly", and to this day they will not regard the equitable market value but insist on taking the assessor's value, although the regulations read that they must adopt whichever is deemed most equitable. Everybody knows that land in British Columbia is overassessed.
I could name several other things. I am sure the government does not want to give the impression that it is chiseling on these old people, and the people do not want the government to do that. However, you must go around and yell at them for a year or so, and perhaps in the end the government will give way.
When the act was first passed it read that the pension was to begin from the date of the man's first application. What did they do? They changed it by regulation to make the pension start from the day the board made its decision that the wretched man was entitled to it, and if they could prove that the poor man at some time was in Africa or some other remote place they kept writing to him for certificates on different things so that his grandchild would be more likely to get the pension than he would. And when they finally had decided, payment was made only from the date when it was decided to give it to him. I have known a man to wait for eight or nine months for his allowance, living, meanwhile upon the charity o^ friends, and when he got his pension he was not able to pay the arrears for board and lodging because the pension was dated back only to the time when they decided that it was due.
Several other matters of this kind occur tome. By just going through the regulations the committee, I am sure, could make useful and reasonable recommendations. The government would have power to say yes or no; they could decide whether they approved the committee's suggestions; they could insist, the next time these local boards got together, on something like ordinary common sense being introduced. So that I say a great deal might be gained by the government allowing this matter to go to the committee. The government has a majority on the committee; I cannot see why they need fear our doing anything unreasonable about it, and it would certainly satisfy a great many people as regards the treatment they are getting, or not. getting, under these regulations.

I suggest that the Minister of Finance do the same thing with respect to one of the regulations to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has just referred. I have in mind section 20 of the regulations which indicates when a pension shall commence. It states that the pension shall commence on the first day of the month following the month in which all necessary information and proof has been furnished, to the satisfaction of the pension authorities, or on the first day of the month following the month in which the applicant first becomes entitled, whichever is later.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni points out, this means that when the applicant for old age pension produces his evidence establishing his eligibility for a pension on the day he becomes seventy years of age, his pension is not made retroactive to the day he became seventy. It becomes effective only on the first day of the month after the month in which he finally got in all those documents to prove his eligibility at the age of seventy.
I know the provincial legislature of Manitoba has discussed this matter and feels that it is quite unfair. I know a resolution was sent down some time ago-probably it has been sent more than once-from the legislature of Manitoba asking this government to change the regulation. That is a regulation which is not in the act, mind: y0U. But as yet nothing has been done. The province of Manitoba is still in a position to say, "We would do it, but for this federal regulation." I suggest again to the minister that he ask his officials who administer the Old Age Pensions Act to go through a number of these regulations to which his attention has been called in the debate. I know the minister may point out that that makes it more patched up, perhaps, than it is already. It is pretty badly patched right now, and if these little adjustments would improve the situation, and take care of some of the grievances, then at least it means something to the old people in the meantime, many of whom will not live for that finer old age pension set-up, which we hope yet to see realized.
There are a number of minor points like that. For example, as I have pointed out

before, if a person, were born on the second day of the month, assuming he gets all the documents in on time, when he becomes seventy years of age and eligible for old age pension that pension could not commence- not according to the act, but according to these regulations-until the first day of the month after the month in which he became seventy. So that many a poor old person who may reach his seventieth year on the second or third day of the month is quite disturbed when he discovers that his pension does not become effective	until	the first	day of	thefollowing month,	and	that the	cheque	willnot be received	until	the 30th	or 31st	dayof that following	month. to the old age pensioner, are two months for which he thought he was going to receive a pension. The amount of money involved1 is not very great. provincial conference, whenever it meets, the whole question of a better and more adequate old age pension scheme, and when in that connection he makes reference to the set-up in New Zealand, I would suggest to him that the mistake be not made again of setting up only a partial scheme. Reference has been made frequently to the opposition to a contributory scheme in this country, as compared with the well-known fact that in New Zealand the people gladly contribute. What is the difference? Is it because of a great difference between our people and the people over there? I think one of the real differences is that any schemes which have been talked about in this country have been partial-just old age pensions, or just unemployment insurance, or just health insurance. All one sees he can get as a taxpayer or as a worker, for his contributions, is protection against only one of the things which may happen to him.

The other point made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is that we

speechtext: In 1926; but rightly or wrongly I gave that principle a great deal of consideration at the end of 1941 when the hon. member for Comox-Alberni urged us to do the same thing about the additional $5. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to make a statement on this. A statement never has been made to the house, and I feel that the country is indebted to the millers for the cooperation they have given in this matter.
These payments relate to the maintenance of the price ceiling, but are shown separately because they are administered by the Canadian wheat board on behalf of the Minister of Finance. As hon. members are aware, flour prices are not permitted to rise above those prevailing in the base period, September 15 to October 11, 1941. Wheat prices, however, have not been subject to the same degree of control; and when in August, 1942, the Canadian wheat board initial price was raised to ninety cents for No. 1 northern in store, Fort William, flour millers were subjected to a serious squeeze. After an investigation by the wartime prices and trade board into milling costs it was decided to make payments to flour millers and other manufacturers of products using western wheat in respect of their domestic sales at a rate equal to the difference between the average monthly price of No. 1 northern wheat and 77$ cents, which was the highest price recorded in the base period when flour ceilings came into effect. This basis of payment was in effect for the year beginning August 1, 1942.
An important change in the basis of payment was made on August 1, 1943. It had been recognized that millers could not be
expected to produce flour for sale in the domestic market if they were unable to obtain western wheat at prices appropriate to the flour ceilings. Some mills, however, as a result of war conditions, were enjoying very large and increased export business, which enabled them to earn excess profits. Most of these increased exports are for Britain and are being financed, in part at least, by Canada. Under these circumstances it was difficult to justify payments to mills earning excess profits even though such profits may be attributable to the export business. After discussions with most of the mills principally affected it was decided to continue payments on the same basis as in the previous year but subject to the refund of any payments contributing to profits taxable at the rate of 100 per cent under the Excess Profits Tax Act. The net effect of this is that the mills will sacrifice the twenty per cent refundable portion of the 100 per cent excess profits tax on any government payments that would have contributed to profits in excess of 1165 per cent of standard profits.
I always intended to say on some occasion, and I want to say now, that I greatly appreciate the cooperation the millers have given the government in this matter.

Housing is an urgent matter to a large number of Canadian citizens, and there is no reason why members of parliament should be deprived from taking advantage of housing legislation. It seems to me that it would be in order to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act to allow members of parliament to enjoy the same rights as any other Canadian citizen to live in houses of their own under the government housing scheme. Members of parliament should not be permitted to take advantage of the legislation to build apartments or houses to rent out. I hope the minister will consider the matter and give his thought to it so that housing of which we hear so much may become an accomplished fact in the near future. To my knowledge people are living in sheds and barns. That may do in the summer but people should have better accommodation than that in the winter. The minister is open-minded and, I am sure, will realize that fact, and I trust that he will consider favourably the suggestion I have made regarding members of parliament and members of the senate as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The difficulty is the Independence of Parliament Act, is it?
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That can be given consideration, but I do not know that we would be justified in bringing in an amendment to the act.

He would be satisfied with a modest little home just the same as the labouring man or anybody else in this country. AH other Canadians can take advantage of the housing schemes, and I do not see why the Independence of Parliament Act should not be amended to permit a member of parliament to

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I know of one landlord who rented a house for S25 a month. The man to whom he has rented it draws S80 a -month from that same house. speechtext: The total mileage of road to which we are committed in the construction is 110 and one-third miles. That includes the road from Rupert to Kitwanga.
Alongside the river.

No; it is alongside the railway, and in some places alongside the river. When this matter was under discussion the other evening it was urged, I believe by almost all members from British Columbia, that the government should be a little more generous in reference to this road in northern British Columbia. I explained to the committee at that time the genesis of the road, and I need not repeat it now. It is true that, if not wholly, 'at least largely the military needs have disappeared.
We hope.

Yes, as we see it at the moment. I have gone into the matter since we discussed it before, and although it is difficult to make a definite statement now, possibly we may be able to save something on the amount appropriated for the maintenance of this 110 miles of road. That depends on weather conditions and on spring freshets which may carry out small bridges and culverts. There is the possibility, however, that the amount estimated may not all be required. If it is not, then I am quite willing

to say to the government of British Columbia that if they will duplicate what we provide for the measure of rehabilitation of the road from Kitwanga to Bazelton, which was the contention advanced the other night, we shall be prepared to go phead. After all, for military purposes we have spent something like $11,000,000 -or will have spent it-on this stretch of road including maintenance. And when the war ends it is scarcely to be expected that the federal government would maintain it. What good will it
be that way?

No; it is not completed.

I am speaking of the section we are completing. This road was built for military purposes. When the military need disappears the road is turned over to the province, without any expense. In effect, what happens is that, because of the military need for this road, British Columbia gets over 111 miles of completed road which cost over $10,000,000, and we are not asking the province to repay any of it.

Well, why should

Will the dominion maintain the road until the conclusion of the war with Japan?

I should like to ask a question. Probably the hon. member for Skeena would like to speak.

The explanation given by the minister seems to be satisfactory. He says they are going to complete the road, and he hopes they will have ways and means to fix up the gaps on the provincial highway. Probably we should not expect him to go farther than that.

I have no objection to that road. On the other hand I cannot see why nothing has been done in connection with an old military road between Riviere du Loup and Madawaska, through Edmundston, and so on. It is an old military road, part of route No. 2, and the government has not done anything in connection with it. For some time money was spent on the trans-Canada highway. The province of Ontario had millions upon millions of dollars, and the province of Quebec had very little. We are now at war. We have a military road in the east, offering the best outlet between the St. Lawrence and the state of Maine. We have as our ally the United States, and there is a good deal of traffic in that locality. When military trucks go to Halifax they pass that way, because it is the shortest route. It is protected, and I cannot see why something is not done for that route.
I now bring the matter to the attention of the minister. He is a broadminded man, and has already done some things at my request. They were not big, in themselves, but I appreciated them just the same as if they had been very big. I hope this time he will realize the importance of this connecting link between the St. Lawrence river, particularly the county of Temiscouata, and the county of Madawaska, from which the Minister of Transport comes.
W'hen one of the minister's lamented colleagues was Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mr. Rogers, some intrigue was made to change the course of that highway. Mr. Rogers would not allow it. He understood the strategic importance of the road. His opinion was most valuable from a strategical point of view, because afterwards he was appointed as the one and only Minister of National Defence, at the start of the war. He had as much military experience in his own head as the three present war ministers have now. And for all those considerations I hope the minister will pay due attention to the matter, consider it and recommend it to his colleagues, for the best interests of this country.

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources

The road to which the hon. member from Temiscouata refers is one that certainly should have consideration in the post-war development of this country. As my hon. friend has quite properly stated, it will be recalled that from 1936 on, the federal government made a contribution to the various provinces to assist in building what were known to be tourist roads, or roads which might serve tourist purposes. I certainly hope-and I am expressing my own personal views-that consideration will be given to that when the war is over.
But the road we are now considering, from Kitwanga to Prince Rupert, was not assisted because it would develop into a tourist route. The purpose of this expenditure was purely military. If that necessity had not arisen I can say to the committee that the government would not have spent a dollar on this road. I hope that explanation will satisfy my hon. friend to some extent.

1 think the minister is halfway to conversion, but I would tell him that the hon. members from British Columbia have insisted all the time that there was a danger to their shores, and so on. I supported them, but when it comes to the east we are very much exposed. The hon. member for Gaspe and I were laughed at when we spoke of the danger. We do not know the future. We do not know what the enemy contemplates doing on the eastern coast. The war is not yet over. The Prime Minister told us not long ago that the war was far from won and that we would still have a long time to fight before it was won. Mr. Churchill said the same thing. I am not asking this from the tourist point of view. I ask it for the army men who travel there in their trucks and bring ammunition and other war materials. I had hoped that the minister would understand it. I know it is easier for him to understand those problems than any one of the three war ministers, and that is why I ask him to-night. I do not object to what has been done for Prince Rupert and British Columbia, but there is a possible danger in the east. I am not a scaremonger, but I can use the same language as western members have used.
You have no Japanese.

No; but the Germans came close to our shores and it is precisely because the hon. member for Gaspe and I insisted on better protection that the danger was not so serious last summer. I will tell the hon. member for Skeena that I do not object to what has been done for his constituency. The
Japanese have their eyes not only on Prince Rupert. We do not know what is in the mind of the enemy. We must be ready to repel any attack, and as we boast of our friendship and amity with the United States the first thing we should expect is good roads to connect the two countries. I would think it foolish to ask something only for my constituency. I do not ask it only for my constituency; I ask it for eastern Canada because it is the best link between United States and Canada. I bring it to the attention of the minister in the hope that something will be done in that regard.

I have one simple question to ask the minister. I understand that a substantial amount of money, something over a quarter of a million dollars, was advanced to contractors to purchase machinery on this road. How much of this money has been paid back and how much remains unpaid?

I cannot hear my hon. friend.

I am not questioning the transaction. I asked if it had been cleared up.

Employment of persons of the Japanese race and/or Japanese nationals, $1,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I will not
detain the committee, and I do not propose to reopen the whole Japanese question because we discussed it the other day and we rested on the promise of the then acting leader of the government that we would have a definite statement of policy from the Prime Minister later on. I am rising to-night only to make a correction in a statement that has been very much circulated. I might pause here for a minute to say I wonder why it is that whenever this subject comes up the information furnished to the public is so very often misleading and invariably misleading in favour of our Japanese enemies. The hon. member for New Westminster in his speech the other day said, I think, that there was a group of officials in Ottawa

I do not exactly know how he put it -who were very, very sympathetic to the Japanese. I begin to think he is right.
As I say, why is it that information is always or often at any rate false and apparently so absolutely innocent. The other day the Minister of Labour made this statement. I am sorry he is not in his seat at the moment, but before I say what I am going to say, may I say that I am perfectly certain he did not intend to deceive the house when he made his statement. He is not built that way. Before he made the statement he expressed sympathy with our point of view. He said, as reported in Hansard, that seventy-five per cent of the Japanese in the dominion were born here. Well, that is absolutely and entirely false. That is all that is wrong with that. The correct figure is twenty-eight per cent-a vast difference. Once you start a lie going, goodness knows how far it will go. I repeat that the minister did not make that false statement wilfully. He just repeated what somebody else had handed him. Some day in the distant future perhaps we shall be able to get around to those officials alluded to by the hon. member for New Westminster and deal with them adequately. Look how it spreads. Here is an article in " Canada at War." It is supposed to be an accurate description, of course, of our efforts in action in the war. This is what appears on Page 55:
Seventy-five per cent of the Japanese in Canada are Japanese-Canadians.
That is, born in Canada, as stated by the Minister of Labour. As I say, the only trouble with that is that it is entirely false. There can be no doubt about that. I have in my hand a

booklet called " Removal of Japanese from the Protected Area in British Columbia." It is a report issued by the British Columbia security commission. They knew all about it, if anyone did. Here is what they say on page 3:
In March of 1941 the many thousands of Japanese domiciled in Canada, practically all of whom were in British Columbia, had been required to register themselves with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the resulting records reveal the following details: Canadian born 6,727, naturalized 7,011, nationals-
That means Japanese not naturalized.
-9,758; United States citizens 16; total 23,512.
If you analyse those figures you will find that instead of seventy-five per cent being Canadian born, it is only twenty-eight per cent. Why the difference? Oh, if you trace it down far enough somebody will say, "We made a mistake," but why are the mistakes always, on the one side? This pamphlet is circulated far and wide; it goes across the country, to our men in the trenches and everywhere else. "Oh," they say, "do not make a fuss about it; seventy-five per cent of the Japanese are born in Canada." It is not seventy-five per cent but only twenty-eight per cent.
Here is something else which was just put in my hands, and remember that I do not go around hunting for trouble. Not long ago the hon. member for Peterborough West asked for a return showing the Japanese who have been allowed to remain in the protected area, out of which they were all supposed to be moved. The return brought down-and I did not ask for it-showed something like ninety-seven. I glanced over the list, and was attracted by the occupations of these people who have been allowed to remain in a protected and therefore dangerous area. Some of their occupations are: aircraft fitter; Empress hotel laundry; retired; no occupation; lawyer; warehouse foreman; cook-house employee; tap dancer-you will readily understand the necessity for having a tap dancer remain in this area-floor lady; factory worker; candy packer; dentist, and so on. I thought there was something funny about it, and took it upon myself to write the department concerned and ask why it was necessary to have so many Japanese in that area. They wrote back and said that they had looked into the thing and that there had been a mistake of forty, that some forty of these people should not have been on the list. Can they not bring down a return covering ninety-seven people without being wrong about forty of them? If I had not dug into that it would have gone out to the world, whatever object they sought to achieve by making this mis-

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
leading statement in a return brought down at the request of the hon. member for Peterborough West.
I rose for the purpose of putting hon. members straight about that seventy-five per cent, but while I am on my feet perhaps I may be permitted to present something else to the committee which came to me not half an hour ago. I have in my hand a copy of a bill introduced in the house of representatives at Washington on May 9, 1944, not a month ago, by Mr. Mott. The bill is, "To provide for the deportation of Japanese aliens." I quote the first sentence of section 2:
Within thirty days after the approval of this act the attorney general of the United States shall proceed to prepare warrants for the deportation of all undesirable aliens as defined in section 1 of this act.
I think it was the minister now before us who told us the other day that to a large extent we would have to be guided by the policy of the United States in regard to the Japanese. Well, this is a sample of that policy. Of course this bill has not been passed as yet; it was introduced only three weeks ago, but at least it is evidence of what some thinking and perhaps foresighted men in the United States congress are doing. I must correct myself. It was not the minister now before us; it was the then acting leader of the government who said that we would have to be guided to some extent by the policy adopted by the United States. How many Canadians are there?

I am advised that the total number at the present time is approximately 800. That number may increase. In countries such as France, Belgium, Holland or Denmark, for example, Canadian nationals may have been able to get along on their own resources, but as those resources become exhausted they ask for assistance, and that assistance is given under this vote through the agency of our protecting power in Europe.
What type of assistance is given? Of course it may be a money grant, but for what purpose?
In the main it is money that is transferred to them so that they can have it available to buy food and other necessities in the places where they live.
And how many did the minister say there were?
About 800.
Does the Lisbon agency have anything to do with that?
No; it is done by Canada's protecting power, which is Switzerland.

I have a certain amount of sympathy for the hon. member for Charle-voix-Saguenay. If this item has nothing to do with immigration, why is it here under the immigration branch rather than under the Department of External Affairs?
Because external affairs requested the immigration branch of the Department of Mines and Resources to handle these funds.
Why?

I do not know why; perhaps my hon. friend should put that question when the external affairs estimates are under consideration. However, I am told that before the war, even in peace time, there was a small fund available in the Department of Immigration for the relief of distressed Canadians abroad. That has always been under the administration of the immigration branch, so that when we came to the larger question, of relief for Canadian nationals abroad it also was handled through the immigration branch.

I submit that the item mentioned by the minister was in the estimates before the war; I remember that very well, because I had an argument about it one afternoon at three o'clock with Mr. Gordon, who was the minister under Mr. Bennett. It seems to me that this item should not come under either the Department of Mines and Resources or the Department of External Affairs. I believe it should come under the Department of National War Services, because the work is done by the Red Cross, and Switzerland is the country where the Red Cross has its headquarters. I do not see why we maintain a civilian vote to look after these people during war time. I have no objection to helping Canadians who are in occupied Europe, but it seems to me that the logical way to help them would be through the Department of National War Services, since the work is carried on through Switzerland.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
